article.headline: Twenty-Five Rules From Monk That Still Hold the Beat
article.lede: In 1960, saxophonist Steve Lacy spent four months playing in Thelonious Monk's band and came away with something beyond musical experience: a handwritten list of directives Monk had given his sidemen, now known as *T. Monk's Advice*. The document has since circulated among musicians, educators, and jazz devotees as one of the clearest windows into how a genuinely original mind thought about making music. What looks at first like backstage housekeeping reveals, on closer reading, a coherent philosophy of art.
article.body:
The twenty-five tips span the mundane and the metaphysical without distinguishing between them — which is part of the point. **"Make the drummer sound good"** sits beside **"a genius is the one most like himself,"** and the juxtaposition is not accidental. Monk believed that self-expression and ensemble service were the same obligation approached from different angles. You could not be fully yourself if you were not listening; you could not truly listen if you had not found your own voice.

Several of the practical directives carry compressed lessons in jazz craft. "Just because you're not a drummer, doesn't mean that you don't have to keep time" is aimed at a specific failure mode: the melodic instrumentalist who treats *rhythm* as the rhythm section's problem. Monk's remedy — "pat your foot and sing the melody in your head when you play" — is the oldest internalization exercise in the tradition, but his insistence on it signals how seriously he took pulse as a shared responsibility.

"Stop playing all those weird notes — play the melody" is startling coming from the man whose own harmonic vocabulary was among the most dissonant in bebop. The instruction is not anti-complexity; it is anti-decoration. Monk's dissonances served melodic purposes; ornamentation that obscured the tune served nobody. The same economy runs through "don't play every time; let some things go by — some music is just imagined that way." *Negative space*, the deliberate rest, is itself a musical statement.

The most celebrated line — "a genius is the one most like himself" — doubles as an implicit critique of imitation. Jazz in 1960 was full of musicians who had absorbed Charlie Parker or Dizzy Gillespie so thoroughly that their own personality had been compressed into a set of borrowed gestures. Monk, whose angularity was often dismissed as amateurism before it was recognized as mastery, had survived that pressure by being stubbornly, recognizably himself. The aphorism is hard-won advice, not a bumper sticker.

"It must be always night, otherwise they wouldn't need the lights" is the document's most poetic entry and the hardest to paraphrase. It acknowledges that jazz clubs are, by design, creatures of darkness and illusion — that the art exists partly *because* of the need for refuge from the ordinary day. Monk's world required that kind of atmosphere to breathe, and he was under no illusion about it. The note to "stay in shape — sometimes a musician waits for a gig, and when it comes, he's out of shape and can't make it" brings things back to earth: beauty is also labor, and labor requires maintenance.

concepts.definition: Jazz-era slang for 'all right' or 'alright,' derived from the 1940s jive vocabulary popularized in swing and bebop circles. Appearing on the list as an interjection, it signals casual affirmation in the argot of the musicians Monk was addressing.

Jazz slang for musicians, in use from at least the swing era. On the list Monk uses it in 'get cats interested enough to come to rehearsal,' meaning fellow players. The word implies a peer relationship — you are one of them, not above them.

In jazz parlance, 'the inside' typically refers to the bridge — the contrasting middle section of a standard 32-bar song form (often the B section in AABA structure). Monk's note that 'the inside of the tune is the part that makes the outside sound good' means that how you handle the bridge determines whether the surrounding A sections land with impact.

In jazz, 'to swing' describes a rhythmic feeling — a forward propulsion generated by the interplay of musicians staying in the groove. It is easier to feel than to define, which is why Monk's advice ('when you're swinging, swing some more') amounts to: once you have the feeling, deepen it rather than second-guess it.

Jazz slang meaning to approach or solicit someone for a job or performance booking. Monk's instruction — 'don't sound anybody for a gig, just be on the scene' — advises against hustling: show up, be visible, let work come to you rather than chasing it.
